lines: Evaluation of anemia discovered incidentally during a workplace screening
He reports feeling well and denies fatigue, weakness, lightheadedness, palpitations, or shortness of breath.
He exercises four times per week, works as a software engineer, and has never experienced limitations in his physical endurance.
His bowel movements are regular, and he denies any change in stool color or consistency.
Based on those findings, he was empirically started on oral iron by a local clinic.
He now returns for follow-up, reporting that he has been taking the iron supplement as directed for six weeks without any changes in how he feels.
Active Problem List:
- Ankylosing Spondylitis
- Beta Thalassemia Minor
- Recurrent Anterior Uveitis
Home Medications:
- Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks
- Sulfasalazine 1000 mg orally twice daily
No known drug allergies
His family history is notable for a father and paternal uncle who were once told they had “small red blood cells” but never required treatment or transfusions.
His diet is well-balanced and includes meat, grains, and vegetables.
He does not drink alcohol, smoke, or use recreational drugs.
On examination, his vital signs are normal.
He is well-appearing and in no distress.
There is no pallor, jaundice, or scleral icterus.
Cardiopulmonary exam is unremarkable.
Abdominal exam reveals no hepatosplenomegaly.
A complete blood count ordered by his occupational health provider showed anemia with microcytosis.
Repeat labs ordered by his primary care physician again show microcytic anemia with no improvement.
Iron studies demonstrate normal serum iron and ferritin levels.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis is performed, which shows elevated hemoglobin A2 and a mild increase in hemoglobin F.
Lower back pain
The patient returns to the clinic with beta thalassemia minor diagnosed in January 2020 and presents with a 6-month history of lower back pain that is worse in the morning and improves with exercise.
He also reports occasional episodes of mild anterior uveitis over the past year.
The patient has tried multiple courses of ibuprofen with minimal relief of his symptoms.

- Ankylosing Spondylitis
- Beta Thalassemia Minor
- Recurrent Anterior Uveitis
Home Medications:
- Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks
- Sulfasalazine 1000 mg orally twice daily
No known drug allergies
He has a family history of psoriasis but denies any personal skin problems.
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Software engineer.
On physical examination, there is decreased lumbar flexion and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints.
His inflammatory markers, including C-reactive protein and erythrocyte sedimentation rate, are elevated.
HLA-B27 testing is positive.
Radiographs of the sacroiliac joints show bilateral sacroiliitis.

His family history is significant for psoriasis in his mother.
Smoking: Never smoker. Alcohol: None. Occupation: Software engineer.
His vital signs are within normal limits.
On physical examination, there is decreased lumbar flexion and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints.
Laboratory tests reveal an elevated C-reactive protein (CRP) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), but HLA-B27 testing is pending.

Chronic lower back pain
The patient is a 29-year-old male with ankylosing spondylitis initially diagnosed in January 2021 and beta thalassemia minor who returns to the rheumatology clinic for ongoing management.
He presents with chronic lower back pain that has been progressively worsening over the past 2 years.
He describes the pain as dull and deep, centered around his lower spine and hips, and notes that it is worse in the mornings or after prolonged rest but improves with physical activity.
He has recently started experiencing stiffness that takes about an hour to resolve upon waking.
He denies any trauma or recent physical strain.
On further questioning, he mentions occasional eye redness and discomfort over the past few months that resolved spontaneously.
Active Problem List:
- Thalassemia minor (diagnosed 2020-01-15)
- Ankylosing Spondylitis (diagnosed 2021-01-15)
- Beta Thalassemia Minor
- Recurrent Anterior Uveitis
Home Medications:
- Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneous every 2 weeks
- Sulfasalazine 1000 mg orally twice daily
No known drug allergies
There is no family history of autoimmune disease, but his father had a “bad back” that required surgery in his 40s.
He works as a software engineer and leads a sedentary lifestyle.
He denies fevers, chills, or weight loss.
Physical examination reveals decreased lumbar spine flexion, reduced chest expansion, and tenderness over the sacroiliac joints.
His gait is normal, but Schober’s test is positive.
Laboratory studies show elevated inflammatory markers, but rheumatoid factor and ANA are negative.
Radiographs of the spine demonstrate changes suggestive of sacroiliac joint sclerosis and fusion.
